## Common Factor Model

![Figure 1](/Users/aginigue/Downloads/Common_Factor_Model.png)

Figure 1 shows an example of the common factor generating model. There
are four latent variables (${\eta_{1}, \ldots}, \eta_{4}$). Directed
edges with arrows represent loadings and undirected edges represent
partial correlations. The first three variables each have a single
indicator that loads at 0.9. The variable, $\eta_{4}$, has two
indicators, with $X_{4}$ loading at 0.9 and the loading ($\lambda_{5}$)
of $X_{5}$ allowed to vary. All indicators have unit variance
($\sigma^2_{\epsilon_{1}}, \ldots, \sigma^2_{\epsilon_{5}}$) given by
$1-\lambda^2$.

## Composite Model

![Figure 2](/Users/aginigue/Downloads/Composite_Model.png) Figure 2
shows the composite generating model. Here, there are 5 latent variables
with $\eta_5$ orthogonal to every other variable. The two indicators
that form a composite are $X_4$ and $X_5$ and have no measurement error.
The factor loading of both indicators are equal in magnitude and is
allowed to vary. Their loadings are computed such that each indicator
will have unit variance and their covariance will be equal to
$\lambda^2$. All other indicators have unit variance
($\sigma^2_{\epsilon_{1}}, \ldots, \sigma^2_{\epsilon_{5}}$) given by
$1-\lambda^2$.

## Unique Variable Model

![Figure 3](/Users/aginigue/Downloads/Unique_Variable_Model.png) Figure
3 shows the unique variable model. There are 5 unique latent variables
with $\eta_5$ acting as a duplicate of $\eta_4$. Each variable is
measured by a single indicator.The loading ($\lambda_5$) of $X_5$ is
allowed to vary to form different levels of redundancy as found in the
other two generating models. All indicators have unit variance
($\sigma^2_{\epsilon_{1}}, \ldots, \sigma^2_{\epsilon_{5}}$) given by
$1-\lambda^2$.

## Bias in Strength Centrality Measure

These simulations are based off 120 conditions each run for 100
iterations. For each generating model we apply three solutions (i.e.,
composite, LNM, or node removal) to every $\Sigma$ correlation matrix.
The mean latent correlation conditions are averaged for each level of
sparsity (i.e., 0.1, 0.3, 0.5 $\ldots$, 0.9 is averaged over a sparsity
of 0, 0.3, 0.5, or 0.7.). The columns (from left to right) correspond to
the redundancy level (i.e., the strength between the duplicated nodes;
0.7, 0.85, or 0.9) and the rows correspond to the size of the network
*p* (10 or 20). The error bars represent one standard error above and
below the mean. For all local centrality measures, bias is computed in
relation to the *target* ($p\text{th}$ node), or the node that is
duplicated to create redundancy with the *clone* ($(p+1)\text{th}$
node).

### Goal Network: Composite

![](/Users/aginigue/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/Solutions_P2/strength_bias_composite_sparsity.png)
Across all levels of sparsity and redundancy level, the composite
solution performed as expected (i.e., a bias of 0) when the goal network
was composite. When sparsity was not induced, LNM consistently had
larger bias, especially in a larger network (*p* = 20). This may be due
to the greater number of parameters needed to be estimated when sparsity
is not induced. We did not see this same pattern in the composite and
node removal solution because they performed simple transformations of
the $\Sigma$ correlation matrix. In contrast to LNM, node removal
consistently underestimated the strength of the target node, although it
was comparable to the composite solution expect under a redundancy of
0.7 and 0.85 and a network size of 20. For all solutions, bias improved
as the level of sparsity increased with results generally improving when
half of all possible edges were removed. When *p* = 20 all solutions
apart from composite had greater bias than when *p* = 10. As mentioned
above, this was particularly true for LNM.

### Goal Network: Unique Variable

![](/Users/aginigue/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/Solutions_P2/strength_bias_pseudo_sparsity.png)

The $(p+1) \times (p+1)$ goal network was made comparable to each
solution by taking the average of the target and the clone's edge
weights. *Should this be occurring? Taking the average of two identical
nodes is the equivalent of removing one of them which is why the node
removal solution looks closest. Forming a composite increases our
reliability so that one makes sense to be higher and same for the LNM. I
think is occurring because we are transforming the p+1 X p+1 correlation
matrix to a partial correlation whereas we are messing with it in the
sigma correlation matrix and therefore changing how the final partial
correlations look. For example, in the removal solution there is more
variance explained that can be redistributed to the pth node* Each
solution consistently overestimated the strength of the Target node and
performed relatively the same for all levels of the conditions.
Performance of LNM mirrored the results found when the goal network was
composite. LNM had greater bias when *p* = 20 and no sparsity was
induced. With greater sparsity (sparsity = 0.7) the performance of each
solution improved the most but still showed bias near 0.4. This implies
that even when the network is quite sparse and redundancy does not
exist, applying a solution can still affect the estimation of edge
weights.

### Goal Network: Common Factor

![](/Users/aginigue/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/Solutions_P2/strength_bias_redundant_sparsity.png)

The results revealed that the LNM performed best compared to the other
solutions when no sparsity was induced, specifically when *p* = 20. In
general, variability in the results is due to network size. All
solutions performed comparably under sparsity \> 0.3 with LNM performing
slightly better under weaker levels of redundancy and greater network
size. Importantly, when *p* = 20 and high redundancy (0.9) all solutions
performed similarly when sparsity increased to 0.3, implying that either
solution was useful in retrieving the edge weight's of the target node.
*Unsure why the LNM performs poorly under no sparsity, is it because
you're estimating the same correlation matrix twice using the same model
so you're getting some estimates that are really far off? It does
improve when we have more apparent redundancy. I ended up finding the
culprit, there was an error in the code, when running LNM my true was
identifying using the loadings whereas my function was using the
variances*

## Bias in Closeness Centrality Measure

### Goal Network: Composite

![](/Users/aginigue/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/Solutions_P2/closeness_bias_composite_sparsity.png)

The results for closeness largely agreed with those for strength when
the goal network was composite. A similar pattern arose under conditions
when LNM was applied without sparsity resulting in greater bias. When
*p* = 10 and at a sparsity = 0.7, LNM underestimated the closeness of
the target node. *I wonder if this has something to do with the NAs or
perhaps the edge weights of the peripheral nodes are being estimated to
be smaller than what we see in the composite*. Node removal matched the
composite solution once sparsity hit 50% across all levels of network
size and redundancy level.

### Goal Network: Unique Variable

![](/Users/aginigue/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/Solutions_P2/closeness_bias_pseudo_sparsity.png)

The pattern of results for closeness mirrored that for strength in the
unique variable network. In contrast, closeness showed notable
variability across solutions than strength did. For example, when
sparsity was not induced, node removal performed best across all levels
of *p* and redundancy. As sparsity increased—specifically, when sparsity
= 0.7 and *p* = 10—LNM outperformed the other solutions. Overall, all
solutions overestimated the closeness of the target node in the unique
variable network.

### Goal Network: Common Factor

![](/Users/aginigue/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/Solutions_P2/closeness_bias_redundant_sparsity.png)

*Any differences found for LNM likely do the coding error* Node removal
and the composite solution matched across all conditions. It's
interesting to see that either removing a node or summing up two nodes
results in a fairly close estimate of the target's closeness when we
estimate a sparse network. Notably, node removal and the composite
solution overestimated closeness and had greater bias when the network
was smaller. *Perhaps, taking node removal for example, removing the
redundant node increases the closeness of the target in a much sparser
network because the target may be a more efficient route ie more
variance can be explained by the target now.*

## Bias in Betweenness Centrality Measure

The plots for bias looked quite similar so I will interpret them in one
paragraph. When the goal network was generated from a composite or
unique variable model, the bias in LNM shot up. *I checked the
iterations of the conditions where this is occurring and it seems that
every so often the bias will be inflated for conditions where the
sparsity is high, maybe I ran my simulation with the old betweenness
function computing relative bias because under normalization the
betweenness value should be bounded betweene 0 and 1? Solution, delete
the edge rather than zeroing it (as I realized 0ing it keeps it in the
network and causes problems when computing betweenness)*

## RMSE of the Target Node's Edge Weights

Root mean square error (RMSE) measures how far our estimates are from
the true value by taking the square root of the average squared
differences. In each plot, RMSE is computed for the target's edge
weights (i.e., how well does each solution recover the edge weights of
the target in the goal network)

### Goal Network: Composite

![](/Users/aginigue/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/Solutions_P2/RMSE_composite_sparsity.png)
These results matched strength. Composite matched perfectly. LNM
performs poorly under no sparsity, and then improved as sparsity
increased. Likewise, node removal underestimated the true value and
because RMSE is always positve the average values are above 0 but still
closer to the composite solution then LNM.

### Goal Network: Unique Variable

![](/Users/aginigue/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/Solutions_P2/RMSE_pseudo_sparsity.png)
Results matched strength. *This makes sense because strength adds up
absolute direct connections and RMSE is doing something similar in a
way*

### Goal Network: Common Factor

![](/Users/aginigue/Library/CloudStorage/Box-Box/Solutions_P2/RMSE_redundant_sparsity.png)
Quite similar trends to strength just flipped. Again, I think LNM is
being impacted by the error in my code. All solutions performed
comparably under sparsity \> 0.3 with LNM performing slightly better
under weaker levels of redundancy and greater network size.

# Friday

## Notes

[**Changes made**]{.underline}

- Changed `E(est.ig)$weight[abs(E(est.ig)$weight) < 1e-4] = 0` to
  `est.ig = delete_edges(est.ig, E(est.ig)[abs(E(est.ig)$weight) < 1e-4])`
  to remove the edge when computing centrality measures. This change was
  also made to `true.ig` and `true.ig.final` in the function
  `calc.all.metrics()`

- Matched identification argument in `apply.lnm()` with how the goal
  network was being simulated. Identification is now set to "variance".
  Setting the argument to "variance" fixes all latent variances to 1,
  allowing all factor loadings to be freely estimated.

- Within `lnm()` the loading of the `[p+1, p]` indicator is fixed to 0.9
  to better recover estimates of the edges in the goal networks.
  Previously, the loading of that same indicator was fixed to 1 and this
  led to estimation issues such as matrices that were nonsensical (all
  estimates were 0.9). I'm not sure why my fix works better, but my
  intuition says that we now have enough elements to estimate the
  network when the redundancy indicator is fixed to 0.9 (if this is even
  what's going on). When all loadings are set to 1, according to
  [psychonetrics](https://psychonetrics.org/lvm.html) documentation,
  that means all loadings are freely estimated. A 0 means that a loading
  is fixed to 0. There is no information on any other value.

Across all levels of sparsity and redundancy level, the composite
solution performed as expected (i.e., a bias of 0) when the goal network
was composite. Our range is 0.2 to (-0.4). LNM had larger bias than node
removal when the degree of redundancy = 0.7 (*p* = 20) and 0.9 (*p* = 10
& 20) but not when redundancy = 0.7 (*p* = 10) and 0.8 (*p* = 10 & 20).
Node removal consistently underestimated the strength of the target
node, when *p* = 10 and 20, the bias decreased as sparsity increased.
Also, when *p* = 10, under no sparsity, the the bias decreased from -0.2
to -0.1 as the the redundancy grew stronger, this same pattern arose
when *p* = 20, starting at *p* = -0.3 and decreasing to \< -0.2. LNM
performed the best when the sparsity was at the max tested. In general,
the LNM solution performed better than removal at higher levels of
redundancy and sparsity and is the recommended solution here.
